ABSTRACT 
Integrated quantum photonics is rapidly emerging as a transformative platform for realizing scalable, chip-based quantum 
technologies, from secure communication to advanced sensing and computing. At the heart of this revolution are solid-state 
quantum emitters: atom-like light sources embedded in a variety of host materials that enable single-photon generation, quantum 
interference, and spin–photon coupling. We begin by discussing quantum emitters across bulk crystals, van der Waals materials, 
and chemically synthesized nanostructures, highlighting their performance trade-offs and integration potential. We then examine 
nanophotonic cavities that enhance the light-matter interaction, from photonic crystals to metasurfaces and Moiré resonators. 
Next, we discuss fabrication techniques with sub-10 nm precision, including material-specific etching strategies and hybrid 
integration schemes. Finally, we address emerging approaches for deterministic placement, cavity tuning, and on-chip scalability. 
By bringing together insights from materials science, nanofabrication, and quantum optics, this Review provides a comprehensive 
perspective on the design and integration of high-performance quantum emitters for scalable photonic platforms. 
1 
Introduction 
The promise of the second quantum revolution lies in its 
ability to engineer and control quantum phenomena, such as 
superposition and entanglement, for transformative applications 
in computing, secure communication, and sensing [ 1–3 ]. A key 
enabler of this vision is the emergence of quantum materials: 
solid-state systems that host quantum states accessible via optical 
or electronic means. 
The suitability of each material platform and fabrication 
approach is ultimately dictated by the target application: quan- 
tum communication requires indistinguishable photons and 
low-loss waveguides, quantum computing demands scalable and 
uniform cavity-emitter interfaces, while quantum sensing relies 
on materials and nanostructures optimized for stability, coher- 
ence, and environmental robustness. In this Review, we focus on 
the role of quantum materials in integrated photonic platforms, 
which offer a scalable, room-temperature-compatible route to 
building quantum technologies [ 4 ]. Unlike other platforms such 
as superconducting circuits or trapped ions, photonic systems 
leverage the long coherence of photons and the compatibility 
of on-chip photonics with mature fabrication methods. At the 
heart of quantum photonics are solid-state quantum emitters, 
which act as single-photon sources or spin-photon interfaces.

2 
Solid-State Quantum Emitters 
Solid-state quantum emitters have made remarkable progress, 
with various types of emitters and materials platforms show- 
ing promises toward scalable integration. In this section, key 
parameters for characterizing quantum emitters and princi- 
ples of correlated emission dynamics in solid-state systems are 
discussed. Furthermore, we benchmark up-to-date solid-state 
quantum emitters by exploring important performance criteria, 
integration scalability, and prospects of on-chip integration along 
the way (Figure 1 ). 
2.1 
Introduction to Quantum Emitter in 
Solid-State System 
Spontaneous emission of a single-photon emitter (SPE) provides 
the basis for the realization of a deterministic, ideal single photon 
source. The key figures of merit of an ideal single photon source 
are summarized in Box 1 . In the solid-state, such atom-like 
transitions can occur from a variety of systems, and are strongly 
modified by the host crystal environment. Depending on physical 
structures, two main emission mechanisms are mainly occuring 
in the solid-state regime: defect-based and exciton-based emission 
(Figure 2 ). The simplest model is the two-level system with a 
ground state and an excited state created by atomic vacancies, 
substitutional foreign atoms, or crystallographic defects within 
the host material. This enforced separation between consecutive 
emission events exhibits anti-bunched photon characteristics. 
Three-level system with an additional metastable shelving state 
can accommodate a controlled emitter with well-defined timing. 
Alternatively, exciton-based emitters exploit quantum-confined 
electron-hole pairs in nanostructures, leveraging quantum con- 
finement to create discrete energy levels with narrow emission 
linewidths. Both transition processes are substantially influenced 
by the lattice environment. Primarily, it suffers from phonon cou- 
pling, which leads to dephasing and broadening of the emission 
linewidth. In particular, a two-level system arising from defects 
in the crystal lattice (e.g., traps, foreign atoms, and impurities) 
induces shifting local electric field near the emitter, which may 
result in spectral diffusion. Moreover, solid-state emitters produce

BOX 1
Key performance metrics of single-photon emitters 
(1) Purity : The single photon purity refers to the ability to generate true single photons (Fock state |1 〉 ) as opposed to multi-photon 
components. It is quantified by the second-order correlation function g(2)(t), which is measured by the Hanbury Brown–T wiss 
(HBT) experiment. The HBT experiment consists in sending the photon stream to a beamplitter and recording the histogram 
of co-detection events as a function of time interval (t) between two detector signals. With zero time delay (t = 0), the function 
yields the probability of simultaneous detection of two photons. Near-zero values of this function indicate that multi-photon 
emission is suppressed. 
(2) Brightness : In mature, integrated devices, the brightness of a SPE-based source refers to the probability for the source to generate 
and collect one photon, as opposed to no photon, following one excitation of the system, in a single mode at the output of 
the source. For isolated emitters, however, brightness is often employed in a broader sense to describe the efficiency of the 
spontaneous emission, quantified by count rates in the detector under continuous excitation, at saturation of the emitter. The 
emission decay rate, while not taken into account in the first definition, is therefore a main parameter for the second. In both 
cases, it is also influenced by the efficiency of the excitation (off-resonant, phonon-assisted, resonant), photon decay paths, 
emitter blinking and quantum efficiency. 
(3) Indistinguishability : Quantum interference between photons is essential for many quantum technologies, as it enables to 
generate entanglement for applications such as photonic quantum computing or quantum networks [ 5 ]. A standard method 
to test the indistinguishability of photons is the Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) experiment. In this setup, two photons are directed 
onto the two input ports of a beam splitter. If the photons are perfectly identical, they will exit together from the same output 
port due to two-photon interference, leading to the disappearance of coincident detections at the two outputs. A high contrast 
in the HOM interference indicates near-unity indistinguishability. However, solid-state quantum devices face challenges from 
environmental noise such as electrical fluctuations and atomic vibrations that disrupt photon indistinguishability. To address 
this challenge, light sources embedded in specially designed electrical structures, precise laser control, and enhancement of 
emission rates can be considered to minimize the impact of environmental interference.

Overview of Solid-State Systems

emitter source for on-chip photonic platform that is compatible 
with versatile fabrication methods and precise spatial alignment.

and design novel alternatives is imperative for attaining such 
quantum emitter source. The choice of the quantum emitter 
source ultimately depends on the target application. For instance, 
quantum communication networks require ultra-narrow spectral 
transitions (e.g., rare-earth ions at telecom band). In contrast, 
quantum sensing favors the spin properties of defect centers in

3 
Photonic Nanostructures for Enhanced 
Light–Matter Interaction 
While spontaneous emission from atomic (or atom-like) defects 
in the solid-state forms the basis of an integrated single photon 
source, the photon emission is typically isotropic and spectrally 
imperfect, limiting its efficiency and scalability. To overcome 
these challenges, integration into nanophotonic structures such 
as optical cavities is employed to enhance light-matter inter- 
action, increase emission directionality and brightness, and 
enable deterministic photon collection and coupling to photonic 
circuits. In this section, we discuss how photonic cavities can 
shape photon emission and provide examples of commonly 
used structures.

3.2 
Common Types of Cavities 
Various cavity geometries can be employed in the solid state, 
balancing trade-offs between 𝑄-factor, mode volume, scalability, 
and fabrication complexity. 
Vertically emitting structures such as Fabry–Pérot cavities [ 39, 
46–48 ], or circular Bragg gratings (bullseye cavities) [ 49–53 ] 
are experimentally convenient. Fabry–Pérot cavities, as shown 
in Figure 3b , are conceptually the simplest type of photonic 
resonator, consisting of two parallel reflecting surfaces, typically 
implemented as distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) or metallic 
mirrors. The mirrors can be planar or curved, and the cavity 
can be either open, offering tunability, or monolithic, providing 
greater robustness and scalability. Emission is usually directed 
vertically by creating an imbalance between the bottom and top 
DBRs reflectivity, and such cavities typically achieve 𝑄-factors of

They require precise nanofabrication and are highly sensitive 
to disorder. Integrated designs can employ 2D PhCCs, where 
holes are patterned into a thin slab or membrane while out- 
of-plane conf inement is provided by refractive index difference 
(which can involve undercutting the substrate), or 1D PhCCs 
(nanobeam cavities) where the holes are essentially etched in a 
waveguide, enabling straightforward integration with photonic 
circuits. To minimize scattering and improve mode confinement, 
lattice defects in PhCCs often use adiabatic tapering (gradually 
changing the hole size or spacing toward the center), which 
improves mirror reflectivity and reduces loss. High-Q PhCCs can 
provide high Purcell enhancement when the quantum emitter is 
located at the center of the cavity, however evanescent coupling 
to an emitter outside the cavity can also be used a convenient way 
to couple emitter to cavities, at the cost of a lower Purcell factor 
and collection efficiency. 
Finally, structures supporting whispering gallery modes (WGM) 
such as microring and microdisk resonators [ 61, 62 ], confine light 
via total internal reflection along their periphery, supporting a 
frequency comb of high- 𝑄modes that circulate around the res- 
onator edge. WGM resonators offer simplicity and compatibility 
with on-chip light coupling due to their in-plane geometry. They 
can achieve very high (up to > 108 ) 𝑄-factor, although at the cost 
of a high mode volume. They can yield Purcell factors in the range 
of 10–50, although achieving unidirectional emission is nontrivial 
as they support both clockwise and counterclockwise modes. 
Finally, the spatially extended optical modes enable simultaneous 
coupling to multiple quantum emitters placed near the resonator 
edge [ 62 ], making WGM a powerful platform for exploring cavity 
quantum electrodynamics in the many-emitter regime. 
3.3 
Alternative Structures 
Beyond traditional c-QED paradigms that rely on spatially con- 
fined photonic modes in optical resonators, other classes of 
nanophotonic systems offer alternative mechanisms to engineer 
light–matter interactions. These include symmetry-protected 
bound states in the continuum (BICs) and Moiré photonic struc- 
tures, both of which exploit interference and periodicity rather 
than physical confinement to achieve strong optical responses. 
These approaches offer new possibilities for integrated quantum 
optics by enabling highly engineered metasurface designs and 
large-area coupling, for instance with arrays of many emitters. 
Bound States in the Continuum (BIC) metasurfaces [ 63 ] are a class 
of resonant nanophotonic systems that support optical modes 
which, despite having energies that lie within the range of radia- 
tive modes, remain perfectly confined and do not radiate. This 
behavior arises due to destructive interference between multiple 
radiation pathways or symmetry incompatibility between the 
mode and the external radiation field, effectively canceling out 
leakage. These modes can exhibit ultra-high quality factors [ 64, 
65 ] (up to 𝑄 > 106 ) without requiring physical mirrors or deep 
subwavelength confinement. BICs are typically realized in planar 
dielectric metasurfaces composed of periodic arrays of nanores- 
onators (e.g., nanopillars or nanobars), where fine tuning of 
structural symmetry (such as slight asymmetries in geometry 
or spacing) enables the transformation of an ideal BIC into a 
quasi-BIC, allowing controlled radiative coupling. 
In the context of solid-state quantum emitters, BIC metasurfaces 
offer a unique platform for enhancing spontaneous emission over 
large areas [ 43, 66, 67 ], with moderate Purcell factors ( 𝐹𝑝 ∼10 − 
100 ) and highly directional emission profiles. The delocalized 
nature of the modes allows relaxed positioning requirements for 
the emitter, in contrast to highly localized resonators such as 
PhCCs. The planar geometry and compatibility with standard 
semiconductor processing make BIC metasurfaces attractive for 
scalable, wafer-level photonic integration. Challenges remain, 
especially regarding optical losses and efficient photon collection. 
In particular, coupling emission from a metasurface into a single- 
mode fiber or an on-chip waveguide is inherently challenging 
due to the often delocalized nature of metasurface modes, which 
are not naturally suited for efficient single-mode, directional out- 
coupling. 
Finally, Moiré photonics [ 44, 68–70 ] leverage the interference 
patterns formed when two periodic structures are overlaid with 
a small twist angle or lattice mismatch. Originally explored in 
the context of electronic band engineering in twisted bilayer 
graphene [ 71 ], Moiré patterns are now being applied to photonics. 
In Moiré photonic structures, such as twisted photonic crystal 
slabs, long-range superlattices emerge and modify the dispersion 
relation. For a certain angle and design of the slabs, the dispersion 
may become flat over the entire Brillouin zone, causing the group 
velocity of optical modes to drop to zero which induces light- 
trapping at certain sites of the superlattice. As the group velocity 
drops to zero, the local density of states diverges, giving rise to 
theoretically predicted ultra-high Purcell factors. 
Moiré flat-band structures offer a powerful platform for enhanc- 
ing light–matter interaction with embedded quantum emitters. 
The spatially extended flat-band modes provide relaxed align- 
ment requirements compared to traditional photonic resonators 
such as PhCCs and allows efficient coupling even with randomly 
positioned emitters. Moreover, the Moiré geometry is inherently 
tunable: the twist angle can be adjusted post-fabrication to control 
the degree of band flattening, while the photonic crystal slab

4 
Nanofabrication for Scalable Integration 
Nanofabrication is a foundational step in translating quan- 
tum materials and phenomena into functional on-chip devices. 
Unlike conventional photonic platforms, quantum materials and 
single-photon emitter integration introduce unique challenges, 
including the fragility of van der Waals layers, which are often 
small and irregular in shape [ 81–84 ]; fabrication difficulties in 
halide perovskites [ 85, 86 ] and diamond [ 7, 15, 87 ]; the need 
for deterministic emitter placement [ 19, 88, 89 ]; high sensitivity 
to etch-induced damage, contamination, and surface charge 
traps [ 90–92 ]; and the requirement for seamless integration with 
low-loss photonic materials such as SiN, SiC, or Ta 2 O5 [ 42, 93–96 ]. 
These materials are often extremely sensitive to fabrication- 
induced perturbations. For example, TMDC monolayers and 
hBN flakes can be damaged by polymers from resist deposition, 
transfer stamp residues, or charge accumulation [ 97–100 ], while 
plasma etching can degrade near-surface nitrogen vacancies in 
diamond [ 101, 102 ], and defects in SiC are prone to surface 
charging or ion-induced decoherence during processing [ 57 ]. 
Therefore, resist selection, exposure conditions, and etching 
protocols must be optimized to balance pattern resolution with 
emitter preservation. Strategies such as “fabrication-around- 
emitter” workflows [ 52, 103–105 ], pick-and-place or deterministic 
transfer techniques [ 106–108 ], and undercut geometries are 
increasingly adopted to mitigate these risks. 
Driven by the stringent requirements of emerging quantum 
technologies, the field continues to evolve rapidly. Fabrication 
approaches must now not only deliver atomic-scale precision but 
also preserve the optical and quantum coherence of embedded 
emitters, while remaining compatible with scalable integra- 
tion workflows. 
The first part of this section focuses on electron beam lithography 
(EBL) and dry etching as foundational techniques in quantum 
nanofabrication. The second part of the chapter highlights state- 
of-the-art nanofabrication strategies tailored specifically for the 
demands of quantum materials as well as their integration into 
next-generation photonic architectures. 
4.1 
Techniques Based on Electron Beam 
Lithography (EBL) 
Electron Beam Lithography (EBL) is the gold standard for 
fabricating high-resolution photonic structures around single 
quantum emitters. Its ability to reach a resolution of sub-10 nm 
enables the precise formation of metasurfaces, photonic crystal 
cavities, and plasmonic antennas tailored to quantum sources 
such as NV centers, quantum dots, and single photon emitters in 
hBN or transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) [ 109–113 ]. 
The principle of operation and key components of a typical 
electron beam lithography setup are illustrated in Box 2 . EBL 
enables the definition of features well below the optical diffrac- 
tion limit due to the high energy and extremely short de Broglie 
wavelength of electrons, which is orders of magnitude smaller 
than that of photons. A sub 10-nm resolution was achieved 
for dielectric structures [ 123, 124 ], and sub-5-nm resolution for 
plasmonic structures [ 125, 126 ]. However, ultimate resolution is 
limited not by diffraction but by the beam column (see Box 2 ) and 
factors such as beam aberrations, Coulombic repulsion between 
electrons, and forward and backscattering within the resist and 
substrate [ 127, 128 ]. 
Achieving such high-resolution features depends on a complex 
interplay of beam and material parameters: 
(I) Electron optics : An ideal electron source should have high 
brightness, uniformity, small spot size, and stability. Brightness, 
measured in amperes per unit volume per steradian, increases 
the reaction rate with the resist, enabling shorter exposure times 
and higher throughput. However, for high-resolution patterning, 
lower beam intensities are often preferred. For example, 1 nA 
at 120 keV may enable 2.5 nm features, while 50 nA results 
in broader features around 200 nm [ 129, 130 ]. Aberration cor- 
rection improves beam focus, but resolution is also affected by 
the point spread function due to scattering and space-charge 
effects [ 131–134 ]. 
(II) Beam diameter : The virtual size of the beam impacts the 
demagnification needed in the column. A smaller virtual size 
leads to a smaller beam spot size with fewer lenses. While 
smaller beam diameters are desired, proximity effects and sec- 
ondary electron generation blur pattern edges, leading to feature 
broadening beyond the nominal beam width. This is caused 
by energy dispersion of the emitted electrons, which can be 
analogous to white light (broad dispersion) or laser light (narrow 
dispersion). Electron emission sources, thermionic, field emis- 
sion, or thermal field-emission, differ in brightness and energy

reducing exposure area broadening. For instance, HSQ developed

etch resistance. In quantum materials, HSQ is especially valued 
for its low-carbon content and ability to serve as a robust etch

Once nanoscale features are defined by EBL, they must be reliably 
transferred into the underlying material without compromising 
emitter performance. The choice of transfer and etching strat-

integration scheme, as discussed in the following section. 
4.2 
Fabrication Approaches and Etching 
Techniques 
While EBL defines the nanoscale patterns, the choice of fab- 
rication strategy, how patterns are transferred into or onto 
the final material, depends heavily on the quantum material 
platform, desired device geometry, and etch compatibility. After 
development, exposed regions can be processed for etching 
or thin-film deposition, while the resist-covered areas act as 
protective masks. Three representative etching-mask strategies 
commonly used in quantum nanophotonics are summarized 
in Box 3 . Representative implementations of resist-mask, hard- 
mask, and double-mask etching, together with examples of 
suspended structures, are illustrated in Figure 4 , highlighting the 
diversity of fabrication routes used across material platforms from 
Si 3 N4 , and InP to hBN, diamond, and SiC. 
Dry etching, particularly ICP and RIE, remains the dominant 
method due to its anisotropy, scalability, and compatibility with 
high-index photonic materials [ 141–143 ]. However, dry etching 
must be carefully optimized for quantum emitters to avoid dam- 
age, roughness, and contamination that can degrade coherence 
and brightness [ 6, 144 ]. 
Certain quantum photonic structures require partially or fully 
suspended nanostructures, for example, for low-losses devices, 
out-of-plane coupling, membrane integration, or strain engi- 
neering and optomechanical systems [ 3, 165–167 ]. Common 
fabrication routes for undercut and suspended structures are 
illustrated in Box 4 . 
When wet etching is used to remove sacrificial layers, structures 
can collapse due to capillary forces. Critical-point drying avoids 
this by replacing solvents with liquid CO 2 and removing it 
without crossing the liquid–gas boundary [ 168–170 ]. For high- 
aspect-ratio or fragile geometries, dry etching is often preferred 
because it avoids surface tension and provides precise control of 
chemical and physical etch components [ 171–174 ].

4.4 
Additional Process Considerations 
Even with carefully optimized lithography and etching, the 
surface environment surrounding a quantum emitter often ulti- 
mately determines its optical coherence and long-term stability. 
Plasma exposure, ion bombardment, and resist residues can 
introduce fluctuating charge traps, modify defect chemistry, 
or roughen sidewalls, all of which contribute to line broad- 
ening, spectral diffusion, or blinking. Consequently, post-etch 
treatments and surface engineering steps form an essential 
final stage in the fabrication of high-performance quantum 
photonic devices. 
One of the most widely employed approaches for restoring 
emitter quality is thermal annealing [ 188, 189 ]. Depending on 
the material platform, annealing in forming gas, inert atmo- 
spheres, or vacuum can repair plasma-induced defects, desorb 
contaminants, and recover photoluminescence. In SiC and GaAs, 
for example, moderate annealing temperatures effectively heal 
ion-induced lattice damage and stabilize color centers, while 
diamond devices can benefit from higher-temperature treatments 
to remove residual graphitic layers [ 189–192 ]. 
Surface passivation plays a similarly critical role. Atomic layer 
deposition (ALD) of high-quality oxides such as Al 2 O3 or Hf O 2 
has been shown to markedly reduce charge noise by neutralizing 
dangling bonds and providing a stable dielectric environment. 
This approach is particularly effective for SiC, GaAs, and III–
V platforms, where surface states strongly influence the optical 
properties of embedded emitters [ 193–196 ]. Even in van der Waals 
materials, where conformal coatings must be applied with care to 
avoid modifying the monolayer, thin ALD films can substantially 
stabilize emission [ 92, 197 ]. 
Effective cleaning processes are equally important. Oxygen 
plasma, UV/ozone treatment, and solvent cycling can remove 
hydrocarbon residues or redeposited materials originating from 
dry etching or resist processing. Such contaminants are especially 
detrimental to hBN and TMDC emitters, where even a few 
monolayers of polymer residue can induce pronounced spectral 
wandering or reduce brightness [ 198, 199 ]. For these materials, 
gentle cleaning strategies and resist-free processing are often 
preferred to avoid additional chemical modification. 
Together, these post-etch treatments directly influence the local 
charge environment, surface morphology, and chemical sta- 
bility of the host material. Because single-photon emitters 
are exceptionally sensitive to their surroundings, even sub- 
nanometer variations in surface quality can affect coherence 
times and indistinguishability. High-quality quantum photonic 
devices therefore rely not only on high-precision lithography 
and damage-mitigated etching but also on a tailored sequence 
of annealing, passivation, and cleaning steps that ensure a clean, 
stable, and well-controlled emitter environment.

5.1 
Deterministic Placement and Coupling 
Advanced nanofabrication can develop the quantum photonic 
devices with sub-10 nm precision, but emitter–cavity perfor- 
mance ultimately depends on placing the quantum emitter 
exactly at the electromagnetic field maximum. In conventional 
nanophotonics, resonators, waveguides, and antennas can be 
positioned arbitrarily with nanometre accuracy, independent of 
the light source. Quantum emitters, however, typically form 
stochastically with random positioning and variation in size and 
composition [ 206 ], leading a mismatching in spatial or spectral 
alignment to the photonic mode. This mismatch limits light–
matter interaction strength, photon extraction efficiency, and 
reproducibility across devices. 
To overcome this, deterministic placement strategies ensure 
either (i) fabrication around pre-located emitters or (ii) position- 
ing of emitters onto prefabricated structures with nanometre- 
scale accuracy (Box 5 ). In the first method, the emitter’s 
location is mapped by marker-based high-resolution photolu- 
minescence [ 61 ] including wide-field methods [ 103, 200, 207 ] 
for high throughput or cathodoluminescence [ 52, 208 ]. Elec- 
tron beam lithography is then aligned to these coordinates to 
define the surrounding nanostructure. Alternatively, direct in- 
situ photolithography can be employed [ 209 ] at the cost of lower 
feature size. 
In the second approach, defect creation via methods such 
as ion-beam implantation [ 210–212 ], electron-beam irradiation 
[ 27, 201 ] or femtosecond laser pulses [ 213, 214 ] into pre- 
fabricated and characterized nanostructures enable top-down 
deterministic device creation. The precision challenge in the 
spatial cavity-emitter coupling hence is shifted towards the 
defect creation process, limited by fs laser spot size, inter- 
action volume or other defect creation mechanisms. Deter- 
ministic fabrication has also been extended to hexagonal

mechanical perturbation, enabling strong and reproducible emitter-cavity coupling [ 204 ]. 
ii. Integration of emitters into a pre-fabricated nanostructure. Photonic structures are fabricated and characterized, before

ter is positioned at the cavity field maximum, achieving 
enhanced brightness and fourfold emission increase at room 
temperature, and represents a significant step toward scal- 
able, on-chip cavity–emitter integration in van der Waals 
materials. 
Precise spatial alignment alone is not sufficient, since quan- 
tum emitters also show spectral inhomogeneity that must 
be matched to cavity resonances. Pre-characterization of SPE 
one-by-one via photoluminescence allows to measure emis- 
sion spectra, however high-throughput characterization based 
on wide-field imaging requires additional techniques such as 
snapshot hyperspectral imaging [ 200 ] (Figure 5a ) or wide- 
field imaging by wavelength-selective photoluminescence excita- 
tion [ 207 ] to determine emitter location and emission wavelength 
simultaneously. 
5.2 
Emitter-Cavity Tuning 
Even with perfect spatial alignment, fabrication deviation, local 
strain, and environmental fluctuations can shift either the emit- 
ter’s ZPL or the cavity mode, causing detuning that reduces 
Purcell enhancement and photon indistinguishability. Emitter- 
cavity f ine-tuning provides post-fabrication control, allowing 
each emitter–cavity pair to be brought into resonance on 
demand. 
Mechanical deformation alters the lattice potential and refractive 
index of the host material, shifting both the emitter ZPL and 
the cavity resonance. Nanobeams, cantilevers, or suspended 
membranes can be engineered to induce uniaxial or biaxial 
strain [ 215, 216 ], enabling reversible wavelength shifts of several 
nanometres without degrading the emitter linewidth. In partic- 
ular, the atomically thin nature of 2D materials allows highly 
efficient strain transfer, enabling large, reversible tuning with 
minimal force. 
Alternatively, applying electric fields to materials hosting SPEs 
can shift their emission wavelength via the Stark effect, either 
through quantum-confined Stark shifts or electrostatic doping 
to adjust transition energies relative to the cavity mode, and/or 
to other emitters. In van der Waals heterostructures, vertical 
gating can reversibly tune quantum emitters, as well as stabilizing 
the electrical environment, resulting in narrow (lifetime-limited) 
emission linewidth [ 217 ]. 
5.3 
Large-Scale Integration 
Recently, precise cavity fabrication and emitter modulation have 
advanced toward integration-ready platforms. Strategies toward 
integration of cavity-coupled SPEs into large-scale integrated 
photonic circuit for quantum information processing depends 
on the type of SPE, host material and compatibility with other 
material platforms (e.g., in refractive index and transparency 
window). While certain materials such as diamond contain 
high-quality SPE, they are not suitable for quantum informa- 
tion processing. Heterogeneous integration [ 218 ] of SPE-based 
nanodevices into chip-scale manufacturable platforms allows to 
combine high-quality SPEs with mature photonic platforms, and 
provides modularity in the assembly process. This is typically 
realized by a pick-and-place method (Figure 5c ) [ 106, 108 ], in 
which pre-selected nanostructures containing SPEs are trans- 
ferred onto prefabricated photonic devices using micro-assembly 
tools. This process however requires accuracies down to tens 
of nanometres. Silicon nitride is a popular choice as photonic 
processing platform [ 107, 108 ] among other possibilities due to 
record-low losses including in the visible range and maturity of 
the fabrication process, while thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN)

Heterogeneous integration leverages the best qualities of dis-

approaches promise seamless integration by uniting emitters 
and photonic functionality within a single host. Continued 
progress along both directions will be crucial to identify the most 
effective architectures for large-scale quantum information pro- 
cessing. 
6 
Conclusion 
In this review, we have outlined the role of solid-state quantum 
emitters in enabling quantum photonic platforms, which is a 
scalable, room-temperature, and CMOS-compatible pathways for 
the advancement of quantum technologies. 
In the second section, we reviewed the current landscape of 
solid-state quantum emitters, categorizing them into defect-based 
and exciton-based systems. We provided a comparative overview 
across various platforms, including bulk materials (e.g., diamond, 
SiC, SiN), van der Waals materials (e.g., hBN, TMDCs), and 
chemically synthesized materials (e.g., colloidal QDs, carbon 
nanotubes, molecular emitters), and further discussed the key 
figures of merit that define their utility in photonic systems. 
The nanophotonic structures are commonly used to enhance 
the emission from the quantum emitters. This is discussed 
in in Section 3 , highlighting the principles of cavity quantum 
electrodynamics in both the weak and strong coupling regimes. 
We compared widely used cavity designs, including vertical 
(Fabry–Pérot, bullseye) and in-plane (photonic crystal, WGM)

As quantum technologies move toward real-world deployment,

materials and fabrication workflows with scalable, low-loss, and 
CMOS-compatible platforms.

Abstract: Integrated quantum photonics is rapidly emerging as a transformative platform for realizing scalable, chip-based quantum technologies, from secure communication to advanced sensing and computing. At the heart of this revolution are solid-state quantum emitters: atom-like light sources embedded in a variety of host materials that enable single-photon generation, quantum interference, and spin–photon coupling. We begin by discussing quantum emitters across bulk crystals, van der Waals materials, and chemically synthesized nanostructures, highlighting their performance trade-offs and integration potential. We then examine nanophotonic cavities that enhance the light-matter interaction, from photonic crystals to metasurfaces and Moiré resonators. Next, we discuss fabrication techniques with sub-10 nm precision, including material-specific etching strategies and hybrid integration schemes. Finally, we address emerging approaches for deterministic placement, cavity tuning, and on-chip scalability. By bringing together insights from materials science, nanofabrication, and quantum optics, this Review provides a comprehensive perspective on the design and integration of high-performance quantum emitters for scalable photonic platforms.
